newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont chemicals heir's murder trial begins.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont chemicals heir's murder trial begins.

text.p: Millionaire chemicals heir John du Pont acted from within an "abyss of insanity" when he killed Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz, his lawyer told a jury on Monday on the first day of du Pont's murder trial.
Attorney Thomas Bergstrom said du Pont, 58, had suffered from paranoid schizophrenia for years and the disorder reached an intense stage on Jan. 26, 1996, when he shot Schultz.

"What happened that day is simply not in dispute," Bergstrom said in his opening statement in the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas. "John du Pont shot David Schultz, backed his car out of the driveway and went home."
"This case is about a killing for no reason whatsoever at the hand of a man who suffered from a mental disease which took away his ability to know what he was doing was wrong."

When du Pont drove to the Schultz home at the far end of du Pont's Foxcatcher estate, Bergstrom said, "John du Pont drove his Lincoln Town Car out of the front gate of his estate and into the abyss of insanity."

Du Pont is being tried on charges of first degree murder in the killing of Schultz, a coach at a wrestling training facility du Pont had established on the estate. If convicted on the first-degree charge he faces life in prison.
Lead prosecutor Joseph McGettigan said in his opening statement that du Pont killed Schultz for the common criminal reasons of "jealousy, envy, revenge, (and) anger."

"He knew what he did and he knew that it was wrong," McGettigan said. In his statement, he gave new details of the prosecution's version of the killing, including what he said were Schultz's last words.

As Schutlz's widow, Nancy, looked on in the courtroom, McGettigan said Schultz emerged from a car he was working on when du Pont and a security consultant drove up. Schultz then greeted du Pont with the words "Hi, coach."
Du Pont then raised his arm from inside the car, a .44 magnum revolver in his hand, and said, "Do you have a problem with me?" and fired the first of three shots into Schultz before driving away.
Bergstrom said du Pont had been driven by delusions and paranoia, which often centred around Schultz.

He said du Pont believed people lived in his walls and that "mechanical trees" on his estate took things from him. Du Pont also believed himself to be figures including the Dalai Lama, the Christ Child and the last czar of Russia.

Under questioning by Bergstrom, Nancy Schultz read from a description of du Pont she had given police hours after the killing. "He's mentally insane. He hallucinates. He talks about things he hears and sees. He thinks he's the Dalai Lama," she said.
She later told prosecutors in the court that she had not meant to give a legal or medical opinion, and was only repeating reports she had heard from others.
Both sides in the case said tapes of conversations held with du Pont during a 48-hour standoff with police after the killings would provide key support for their positions.
